title: Contrarian debrief: Jamie Ross (Senior Runtime Engineer) - draft
content:
Context: I know the panel leaned towards green for Jamie, but I have a different take. Writing up a contrarian view to preserve nuance and propose mitigations if we still proceed. Candidate applied for Senior Runtime Engineer; loop included system design, live debugging, and a take-home micro-batching task.

High-level takeaway:
- Strengths: Clear mental model of KV cache and attention memory; good on long-context tradeoffs; pragmatic on quantization vs model quality.
- Concerns: shaky on performance debugging (profiling at kernel level), limited exposure to multi-GPU sharding and NCCL pitfalls, and optimistic about deployment automation timelines.
- Recommendation: not a straight hire for Sr role without pairing/reskilling plan. Consider for Senior+Engineer with explicit ramp plan, or strong match for Staff if we can pair with infra lead (contradictory, see rationale below).

Technical signals (examples):
- System design (30m): Proposed an elegant single-host sharded cache with partial replication to reduce cross-host fetches. Pros: latency-focused, simple. Cons: underestimated memory pressure and write amplification; didn't propose backpressure strategies for concurrent writes. When pressed, fallback was to 'increase RAM' — not acceptable at scale.
- Profiling/debugging exercise: Candidate recognized CUDA streaming issues on paper but when given a flamegraph snippet missed the root cause (kernel launch serialization from host-side synchronous memcpy). Repeatedly pointed to batching parameters rather than async memcpy overlap; panel had follow-ups that clarified but candidate didn't pivot quickly.
- Take-home micro-batcher: Clean code, good test coverage, docs. But benchmark harness omitted warm-up iterations and KV-cache-miss scenarios; numbers presented likely optimistic. Their patch to use a global mutex for queue draining is simple but could become a contention point at high qps.

Behavioral / working style:
- Highly communicative and thoughtful in follow-ups; wrote a good design doc after interview with tradeoffs enumerated.
- Tends to default to pragmatic short-term fixes rather than designing for worst-case scale (good for start-ups, risk for our Dedicated customers).
- Shows growth mindset and openness to feedback — strong plus.

Risks and mitigations if we hire:
- Risk: insufficient low-level GPU-performance intuition. Mitigation: 3-month bootcamp pairing with profiling owner + reading list (NVIDIA profiling, NCCL hang diagnostics). Add pairing sessions on oncall rotation.
- Risk: naive concurrency primitives that can cause contention. Mitigation: coding checklist for lock-free patterns, code review gating for hot paths, automated perf regression tests.

Suggested scorecard (my numbers):
- System design: 6/10 (solid concepts, missed scale bits)
- Low-level perf/debugging: 4/10 (needs ramp)
- Code quality: 8/10 (tests and docs are good)
- Communication/collab: 8/10
- Overall: 6/10 -> borderline; hire only with explicit ramp plan and mentorship.

Open questions to resolve before final call:
- How quickly can they demonstrate NCCl sharding debugging on a short pairing task? (pair for 1 day)
- Can they add micro-batcher warm-up scenarios and KV-miss tests within 48 hrs? If yes, re-evaluate perf.
- Confirm willingness to take on oncall shifts during ramp.

Action items I propose:
- Ask candidate for a 2-hour pairing session focused on a perf-debugging scenario (Marcus to take lead).
- If pairing goes well, offer with 'senior' level plus onboarding plan and 90-day success criteria (profiling ownership, one perf regression fix).
- If pairing goes poorly, close loop with candidate and preserve for future-mid level roles.

Links/references inside doc: Linear ticket DEV-342 (take-home), PR #2891 (micro-batcher), Slack thread #hiring-runtime-jan.

Notes to self: keep this draft internal. I expect pushback on the recommendation; panel liked the candidate's product judgment and speed. Still important to flag low-level perf issue before commit.

End of notes.
